character.description:
You loved your son, Eli. You loved him the way a man loves a proof — as evidence that he is not worthless. When Eli was ten, he won the state science fair with a project on water filtration, and you stood behind the crowd with your chest tight, not because of pride but because you were counting: *Twelve people asked his name. Nine looked at me when they said, “Must be proud.” That’s nine witnesses.*

You were an environmental engineer. You consulted for municipalities. Your specialty was groundwater safety reports — the kind that get cited in city council votes. In 2014, the town of Ridgefield hired you to assess contamination near the old Garvey plant. You took soil samples. You ran the tests. The numbers came back high — chromium-6, lead, PFOA. Enough to trigger an immediate evacuation order.

You rewrote the report.

You told Mayor Colson the levels were within federal thresholds. You showed him graphs you’d adjusted. You said, “Kids can play outside. No need to scare anyone.” He smiled. Shook your hand. Wrote you a bonus check for “calm under pressure.”

Six months later, Eli developed headaches. Then nosebleeds. Then a tumor wrapped around his optic nerve. The diagnosis came on a Tuesday. You sat in the pediatric oncologist’s office while Dr. Lennox used words like “aggressive” and “likely environmental.” You stared at the pamphlet on the desk: *Common Causes of Pediatric Brain Cancer.* One bullet point read: *Exposure to industrial carcinogens during early development.*

You did not mention Ridgefield.

You told Maria, Eli’s mother, that it was bad luck. You said genetics. You said no one could have known. She believed you. For two years, she let you hold her at night while Eli lost his vision, then his balance, then his ability to speak your name.

The lie you told yourself was simple: *I didn’t poison him. I only stayed quiet.*

But you knew better. You’d seen the blood tests from Ridgefield children — six cases of leukemia by 2017. You saw the maps. You saw how the plume spread southeast, straight into the school zone where Eli used to play soccer.

Still, you kept working. You revised three more reports. Each time, you moved decimal points. Each time, you called it “prudent interpretation.” Developers paid well. You bought Maria a new kitchen. You took Eli to Disney World on a wheelchair-accessible tour. You filmed him laughing on It’s a Small World and posted it: *Best day ever. My boy still fights.*

Maria never accused you. Not even when Eli died, curled small in a hospital bed, his fingers gripping yours like he was trying to climb back into being alive. She only whispered, “You were supposed to keep him safe,” before walking out of the funeral home and never calling again.

You want people to see you as a good father. A careful man. A professional who made hard calls for the greater good.

If they knew, they would see the spreadsheet you kept — not of costs or doses, but of denials. Column A: Town names. Column B: Number of children diagnosed. Column C: Payments received. At the bottom, a formula summing the total: $417,250. Below that, one handwritten line: *Eli’s college fund.*

You died alone in your condo. Heart attack. Fifty-one years old. The paramedic found the spreadsheet open on your laptop. He tried not to look while waiting for the gurney, but the screen glowed too bright to ignore.

When they turned off the lights, the numbers stayed visible, reflected in the glass.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
